chunks: And my father (may Allah have mercy on him) narrated to me from Sa'd ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Hasan ibn 'Ali ibn Faddal, from Ibn Bukayr, from Zurarah, from 'Abd al-Khaliq ibn 'Abd Rabbih, who said:

I heard Aba 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) say: 'Allah did not give him a namesake before [him]. Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali had no namesake before him, and Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon him) had no namesake before him. And the heavens did not weep for them except for forty mornings.' I asked, 'How did they weep?' He said, 'It rose red and set red.'

key_terms.الْحُسَيْنُ بْنُ عَلِيٍّ: Al-Husayn ibn 'Ali, the grandson of the Prophet
key_terms.سَمِيًّا: Namesake or one who shares the same name
key_terms.يَحْيَى بْنُ زَكَرِيَّا: Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the son of Zechariah)

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of the heavens weeping for forty days in Shia tradition?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (a.s.) highlights the unique nomenclature of Husayn and Yahya, emphasizing their distinctiveness in Islamic tradition, while linking their martyrdom to a cosmic phenomenon where the heavens wept for forty mornings. This celestial mourning, manifested by the sun's red hue, underscores the profound spiritual gravity of their sacrifices in Shia historiography. The narration serves as a theological affirmation of the interconnectedness of heavenly and earthly realms during pivotal moments of divine favor and loss.
